scenario: AITA for calling the police on my daughter to teach her a lesson about stealing? | My daughter is in the sixth grade. Every morning, I have her take a couple of dollars out of my wallet for lunch money. In the last few weeks, several times I have noticed that I am missing a little bit more money than usual. So, this week, I planted a 20 dollar bill before my daughter took her lunch money out. Sure enough, she took it. I called the police and asked them to come with me to the school so that we could teach my daughter a lesson. Two officers met me there and we pulled my daughter out of class, after which she informed one of the officers that there has been a bully who is stealing her lunch money/forcing my daughter to buy her lunch. She also has been buying lunch for one of her friends who can not afford it. This was confirmed by both the bully, and the friend. My daughter was silent on the way home and i informed her that I was just trying to teach her a lesson, that stealing is wrong and can get you in a lot of trouble. and that in the future she needs to speak to myself or her mother if there are issues at school and we would be happy to help her resolve them. When we got home, my wife absolutely lost her shit on me, in full tears, telling me that this is a one way ticket to estrangement from our daughter in the future and that we should have just asked her why she was stealing money. She would have just lied about stealing in the first place so I really don’t understand what her idea of a solution is. My daughter apparently told my wife that she is terrified that her bully will now retaliate, and also that she may have lost her friend for bringing so much attention to her financial issue. She apologized for stealing and said she just didn’t want us to intervene. I am wondering if I really did the wrong thing here. AITA?

message.reasoning: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether calling the police on my daughter to teach her a lesson about stealing was the right thing to do. Let me start by understanding the situation better. My daughter is in the sixth grade, and every morning I give her a couple of dollars for lunch money. Over the last few weeks, I noticed that I was missing a bit more money than usual. So, this week, I planted a $20 bill before she took her lunch money. Sure enough, she took it. I called the police and asked them to come with me to the school so that we could teach her a lesson. When we got to the school, two officers met me there, and we pulled my daughter out of class. She then told one of the officers that there has been a bully who has been stealing her lunch money and forcing her to buy lunch for the bully. She also mentioned that she has been buying lunch for one of her friends who can't afford it. Both the bully and the friend confirmed this. My daughter was silent on the way home, and I told her that I was just trying to teach her a lesson, that stealing is wrong and can get her into a lot of trouble, and that in the future she needs to speak to me or her mother if there are issues at school and we would be happy to help her resolve them. When we got home, my wife absolutely lost it, in full tears, telling me that this is a one-way ticket to estrangement from our daughter in the future and that we should have just asked her why she was stealing money. She said that my daughter would have just lied about stealing in the first place, so I really don't understand her idea of a solution. My daughter apparently told my wife that she is terrified that her bully will now retaliate, and also that she may have lost her friend for bringing so much attention to her financial issue. She apologized for stealing and said she just didn't want us to intervene. I'm wondering if I really did the wrong thing here. AITA? (Am I the Asshole?) Alright, so first, I need to understand the context fully. My daughter was taking extra money, which I noticed. I decided to set up a situation where I could catch her in the act, involving the police to teach her a lesson about stealing. However, when the police arrived, my daughter revealed that she was being bullied and that she was using the extra money to buy lunch for herself and a friend who couldn't afford it. My wife is upset with me for involving the police, thinking that this could damage our relationship with our daughter and that we should have talked to her first to understand why she was taking the money. My daughter is also upset, fearing retaliation from the bully and possibly losing a friend because of the attention brought to her financial situation. So, the question is: Was calling the police on my daughter to teach her a lesson about stealing the right thing to do, or was it wrong? To answer this, I need to consider several factors: 1. **Understanding the Situation**: Did I fully understand why my daughter was taking extra money before deciding to involve the police? It seems like I didn't, as she revealed the bullying and the need to buy lunch for herself and a friend. 2. **Teaching the Lesson**: Was involving the police an appropriate way to teach her about the consequences of stealing? Or was there a better way to address the issue without escalating it to law enforcement? 3. **Impact on Relationships**: How did my actions affect my relationship with my daughter and my wife? My wife is upset, and my daughter is scared and feels that we overreacted. 4. **Alternative Approaches**: What could I have done differently to address the issue more effectively and compassionately? 5. **Long-term Consequences**: What are the potential long-term effects of involving the police in this situation on my daughter's behavior and trust in me? 6. **Ethical Considerations**: Is it ethical to use the threat of police involvement to teach a lesson, especially when the underlying reasons for the behavior were not fully understood? 7. **Legal Implications**: Are there legal implications for involving the police in this manner, especially regarding the privacy and rights of minors? 8. **Emotional Well-being**: How did my actions affect my daughter's emotional well-being, and what steps can be taken to repair any damage caused? 9. **Communication**: How can I improve communication with my daughter and wife to prevent similar situations in the future? 10. **Learning Opportunity**: How can this situation be turned into a learning opportunity for my daughter about handling difficult situations and seeking help from parents? Considering all these factors, it seems like involving the police without first understanding the full context of why my daughter was taking extra money was a mistake. It led to unnecessary stress and potential damage to our relationship with her. Instead, talking to her first to understand her actions and addressing the underlying issues, such as the bullying and her desire to help her friend, would have been a more compassionate and effective approach. Additionally, my wife's reaction indicates that she feels this approach was harmful and could lead to estrangement. It's important to consider her perspective and work together as a family to support our daughter through these challenges. In conclusion, while the intention was to teach a lesson about stealing, the method used was not appropriate given the circumstances. A more understanding and communicative approach would have been better suited to address the issue and support our daughter.
